verses.note: Humanity's first commission is work: filling, cultivating, and ordering the earth. Work comes from the blessing before the fall, not from the curse after it. Genesis 2:15 restates it as working and keeping the garden.

The earth's lack is partly a lack of a worker. Before the man exists, the text already defines part of his purpose: the ground is waiting for someone to serve it. Human labor is written into creation's design, not added after the fall.

Work is given in the garden, before sin, as part of what it means to live well before God. Avad and shamar also describe priestly service at the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8), so ordinary tending of the earth and the service of God are joined from the start.

Work itself is not the curse; it was given in 2:15. What changes is that the ground now resists, and labor becomes toil. Paul says that creation was subjected to frustration and waits for its own release (Romans 8:20-22).

City building begins in the line of Cain, but Scripture does not condemn the city as such; it ends with the city of God (Revelation 21:2). Human culture can be a way of securing oneself apart from God, as at Babel (11:4), or can be gathered into God's purposes.

Music, craft, and animal husbandry are presented as human achievements, not gifts stolen from the gods. Scripture elsewhere credits skill in craftsmanship to God's Spirit (Exodus 31:3-5), so the gifts are good even when their first bearers were far from him.

Laban is right that work deserves wages, and Israel's law later insists on it (Deuteronomy 24:14-15). But the chapter shows how a fair-sounding arrangement can become a means of exploitation when one party holds all the power, a concern the prophets return to (Jeremiah 22:13).

Jacob's account of his labor is a picture of faithful work done for a master who did not deserve it. Scripture elsewhere commends service done well even to unjust masters (1 Peter 2:18-19), and Jacob's complaint shows that faithful work does not require silence about injustice.
